q: How does the effective Trotter order degrade when H is replaced by a longer-range or hopping+interaction fermion model (e.g. Hubbard) after a Jordan-Wigner map, where the even/odd bond split no longer contains all long-range Pauli strings? Does the observed slope 2 persist, or does it drift toward 1 because the long-range JW strings become the dominant non-commuting piece?
basis: Our reproduction saw a clean slope 2.002 on a nearest-neighbour Heisenberg chain where the odd/even split cleanly commutes within each group. That algebraic property is exactly what the paper implicitly assumes for its diag*FFT*diag form, but it fails for fermions after JW.
next_steps: Repeat the same K in {10,20,50,100,200} sweep on 1D Hubbard for n in {4,6,8} qubits post-JW, splitting by (hopping + interaction) vs (parity groups), and refit the log-log slopes to see whether the empirical order drops.

q: For a fixed target error epsilon, at what n does the constant-factor prefactor in Zalka's poly(n,T,1/epsilon) circuit cost first beat a direct 2^n x 2^n classical expm on the same hardware? At n=4, classical wins by many orders of magnitude; the paper does not quantify this crossover.
basis: We measured gold-standard classical expm wall time = 0.0017 s at dim=16. That's an outrageously good classical baseline; the paper's asymptotic claim tells us nothing about where it crosses over on real hardware.
next_steps: Extend the harness to n in {6, 10, 14, 20} using sparse Hamiltonian action + Krylov, and simultaneously estimate quantum gate counts for the same problem using Qiskit's Trotter primitives; report the crossover n_star.

q: Zalka assumes a single monolithic 1D-particle register per degree of freedom. What is the actual Trotter-error penalty from a nested-register encoding in which kinetic and potential registers are physically separated and coupled only through SWAPs? Does the leading-order coefficient inflate by a small constant or by a factor scaling with the SWAP depth?
basis: Our reproduction used dense-matrix exponentials, so we never had to model the SWAP overhead the paper elides. The gap between 'ideal algebra' and 'physical layout' is a real modern implementation cost the paper doesn't quantify.
next_steps: Implement two versions of the same 2nd-order Trotter step in Qiskit: (a) fully connected and (b) linear-nearest-neighbour with explicit SWAP inserts, and compare Frobenius errors at matched Delta t.

q: The paper's 'energy drain' ground-state preparation (Sec. 3.1) is proposed with no analysis of the reset-frequency vs decay-rate tradeoff. On a small 4-qubit Heisenberg target coupled to a 4-qubit drain of gaps {E0, E0/2, E0/4, E0/8}, what reset cadence minimises the time-to-threshold for |<GS|psi(t)>|^2 > 0.9, and how does that scale with system-drain coupling strength?
basis: Our Heisenberg model is the natural playground for exactly the drain protocol Zalka proposes but never simulates. It is inexpensive to test (dim=256 total) and would fill a real gap in the paper.
next_steps: Extend trotter_heisenberg.py with a bilinear system-drain coupling, run 2nd-order Trotter with periodic partial trace + drain reset, sweep reset period in [dt, 20 dt] and coupling in [0.05, 1.0], measure time-to-threshold.

q: Zalka states the QFT costs '~ l^2/2' local gates but does not track the constant, and modern approximate-QFT constructions with banded phase gates drop this to O(l log l). Given the epsilon window verified here (10^-1 down to 10^-4), what banding depth suffices to keep the per-step Trotter error dominant over the QFT-truncation error, and does that change the observed slope-1 / slope-2 behaviour?
basis: Our reproduction validated the pure Trotter slopes with an exact kinetic operator. The paper glosses the exact-vs-approximate QFT question, but for any real quantum-circuit implementation it will be the binding cost.
next_steps: Build an approximate-QFT harness parameterised by banding depth b, insert it in place of the exact kinetic exponentiation, sweep (Delta t, b), and locate the Pareto frontier where the two error sources meet.
